title: Homeless man might still be alive if Taser was used by Vancouver police, inquest told
subtitle: If Vancouver police used a Taser, Michael Vann Hubbard might still be alive today, said the lawyer representing the family of the 58-year-old U.S. citizen, who suffered from schizophrenia and was shot by police.
article: If Vancouver police used a Taser, Michael Vann Hubbard might still be alive today, said the lawyer representing the family of the 58-year-old U.S. citizen, who suffered from schizophrenia and was shot by police.

Speaking at the end of a three day coroner's inquest Wednesday, Doug King said while the use of Tasers is controversial he believes it would have been the right situation in Hubbard's case that "might have saved his life."
Hubbard, a pipe fitter who had moved to Canada a year earlier and was living in a homeless shelter, was shot by police March 20, 2009 after he threatened them with a utility knife.
"It's a difficult question on how and why they (Tasers) should be used," said King.

"But this is the kind of a case a Taser would have worked perfectly. There were two officers there and one could have used the Taser and the other kept the gun on him. Neither officer though had training or access to a Taser."

King said Hubbard's family, who live in Illinois and did not attend the inquest, would have liked a recommendation that at least one of the officers should have been trained and equipped with a Taser.
This was not among the five-person jury's recommendations.
The jury's recommendations instead included:
-Vancouver police require all officers have basic first aid when they are hired and maintain their first aid certification.
-All police cars have a basic emergency first aid kit.
-Vancouver police continue with their goal of training every member in the 40-hour crisis intervention course (which includes how to deal with mentally ill persons).
-Review and upgrade emergency scene protocols as needed to ensure fire and ambulance personal and equipment can get to and leave an emergency scene.
King said the jury heard the ambulance crew that arrived to help Hubbard was blocked by a police vehicle from reaching him.

He said a police officer was with the vehicle at the time, but did not have a key to move the car and an ambulance crew couldn't transport Hubbard to their ambulance parked a block away without first stopping resuscitation attempts.
"His only chance of survival was whether he could have gotten into surgery," said King.
"It was clear from the evidence the police priority was not in giving him medical care but in making sure the scene was secured."
King said another recommendation the family would have liked to see concerned the stereotyping they believe happens with the homeless.
King noted the incident arose after the two Vancouver police were assigned to look for a stolen backpack and immediately went to Balkin House, the homeless shelter Hubbard was living in at the time.
He said since Hubbard had a black bag similar to the one stolen from a car moments earlier an assumption was made he might be the suspect.

Const. Celia Tisdall had testified she asked Hubbard for identification and to examine inside his backpack , but Hubbard responded by asking for her identification. She told the inquest earlier that when she threatened to put him in handcuffs he pulled out the X-Acto knife.
Tisdall said both she and her partner, Const. Estilize Wicks, ordered Hubbard repeatedly to put the knife down but he held onto it and walked towards the officers.
Hubbard's daughter, Kimberly Hubbard, testified by telephone from Illinois earlier Hubbard had an idealistic view of Canada and believed "if he went to Canada, things would be different."
King said the family "want closure and something positive to come from this."
"They want to know the death of their family member wasn't in vain," he said.
But King said he personally doesn't believe this will prevent other police shootings of mentally ill persons in Vancouver.

"About one third of all shootings by police involve mental health illness calls. They are undeniably a large part of police deaths. Certainly we've seen them before and we will see a few after," he said.
